subChunks.title: Lead Capstone — Enterprise Product Page
subChunks.hookHtml:
This is the Lead capstone. Everything you have learned at this tier — the agency commission, Tailwind internals, v4 migration, Next.js integration, advanced typography, accessibility audit methodology, complex animation orchestration, the Figma pipeline, enterprise design system architecture, build pipeline optimisation, and cross-platform tokens — converges in a single deliverable. A complete enterprise product landing page, built to professional production standards.

This is not a practice exercise. This is the standard of a Lead engineer's output.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon: "A Lead engineer's output is not distinguished by the number of utilities they know. It is distinguished by the quality of their decisions. Why sticky, not fixed. Why ring, not border. Why semantic tokens, not arbitrary values. Why motion-reduce paired with every animation. Why sr-only on every icon-only button. These are the decisions that separate competent work from excellent work."

The Lead capstone requirements

The page must demonstrate every lead-tier principle:

  • CSS-first v4 architecture: @theme tokens, no hardcoded hex, @variant dark
  • Three-level token hierarchy: primitive → semantic → component
  • Accessibility: focus-visible rings on all interactives, sr-only for icon buttons, colour contrast ≥4.5:1, motion-reduce paired with all animations
  • Typography system: fluid heading with clamp(), max-w-prose for body, correct leading at each size
  • Complex layout: CSS Grid with auto-fill for the features grid, container queries on the testimonial card
  • Animation: staggered entrance with animation-fill-mode:both, motion-reduce:animate-none on all
  • Dark mode: three-state (system/light/dark) with correct dark: variants
  • Responsive: mobile-first, tested at 375px, 768px, 1280px

Page structure

1. Sticky frosted-glass nav
   - Logo, nav links (hidden on mobile), dark mode toggle, CTA
   - All nav links: focus-visible rings

2. Hero section
   - Gradient background, fluid heading, gradient text span
   - Two-column at lg: text left, visual card right
   - Primary CTA with brand-shadow, secondary ghost CTA
   - Staggered entrance animation

3. Features grid
   - grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(280px,1fr))]
   - Each card: group hover, icon group-hover colour change
   - Container query on description visibility

4. Testimonials
   - Two-column at md
   - Avatar: object-cover, ring frame, relative/absolute status dot

5. Pricing section
   - Three cards: free, pro (featured with ring-2), enterprise
   - Featured card: ring-2 ring-primary ring-offset-2

6. Footer
   - Four-column grid, condensed links, WCAG-compliant contrast

Quality checklist

□ axe DevTools: 0 violations
□ Keyboard navigation: every interactive reachable and visible
□ CSS bundle: <30KB gzipped
□ Lighthouse accessibility: 100
□ All animations: motion-reduce:animate-none paired
□ Dark mode: all sections correct in dark
□ Mobile: no overflow at 375px
□ Semantic HTML: nav, main, section, article, footer
□ No hardcoded hex colours: only tokens or standard palette
□ Every icon-only button: aria-label or sr-only

Lyra the Scribe: "When you deploy this page to a public URL, you are making a claim: I know this craft at the lead level. That claim is either supported by the evidence — the URL — or it is not. The checklist is not bureaucracy. It is the minimum standard of evidence."

storyBeats.text: The grand hall is empty except for Solomon, who stands before the projection of the completed commission. He studies it for a long moment. The silence is different from before — it is not expectant. It is evaluative.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: The question I ask of every Lead candidate is not 'can you build this?' Any competent Senior can build this. The question is: 'can you build this correctly, explain every decision, and defend every trade-off?' That is the Lead standard.

storyBeats.speaker: Lyra the Scribe
storyBeats.text: Review the checklist before you submit. Not to prove compliance to me — to prove it to yourself. If you cannot check every box with confidence, you know exactly what to study next.

storyBeats.speaker: Sable the Illuminator
storyBeats.text: Build it. Ship it. Point to it. This is what you can do.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build the complete enterprise product landing page. Apply all Lead tier principles — every section, every interactive, every token, every animation pairing. This is the full synthesis.

Required selectors and their constraints:

  • .ent-nav: sticky, top-0, z-50, bg-white/90, dark:bg-gray-900/90, backdrop-blur-md, border-b, border-gray-200, dark:border-gray-800
  • .ent-hero: bg-gradient-to-br, from-indigo-950, via-purple-950, to-slate-900, py-24
  • .ent-hero-heading: text-5xl, lg:text-6xl, font-extrabold, text-white, leading-tight
  • .ent-gradient-text: text-transparent, bg-clip-text, bg-gradient-to-r, from-indigo-400, to-purple-400
  • .ent-features-grid: grid, grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(280px,1fr))], gap-4
  • .ent-feature-card: bg-white, dark:bg-gray-900, rounded-xl, border, border-gray-200, dark:border-gray-800, p-6, group, hover:shadow-md, transition-shadow
  • .ent-cta-btn: bg-indigo-600, hover:bg-indigo-700, text-white, font-semibold, px-6, py-3, rounded-lg, transition-colors, focus:outline-hidden, focus-visible:ring-2, focus-visible:ring-indigo-600, focus-visible:ring-offset-2
  • .ent-pricing-featured: ring-2, ring-indigo-500, ring-offset-2
  • .ent-avatar: w-12, h-12, rounded-full, object-cover, ring-2, ring-white
  • .ent-sr-label: sr-only

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
The final act of the Lead commission: build and deploy.

Build the complete enterprise product page from scratch — no starter code, no scaffold. Apply every principle from the Lead tier. Deploy to a public URL (CodePen or GitHub Pages). Run axe DevTools and confirm 0 violations. Check every item on the quality checklist manually.

When done, your deliverable is two things: the live URL and a brief audit report (5-10 bullet points) describing the decisions you made and why — not what you built, but why you built it the way you did. A Lead engineer can always explain their decisions.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Review the enterprise product page you just built. Select five technical decisions you made — not just 'I used focus-visible:ring-2' but 'I used focus-visible:ring-2 rather than focus:ring-2 because focus-visible only activates on keyboard navigation, not mouse clicks, which prevents the ring from appearing on mouse-click which is visually distracting.' For each decision, explain: what you chose, what the alternative was, and why your choice was correct for this context.

questions.prompt: The enterprise page uses dark:bg-gray-900/90 on the nav. A junior engineer suggests removing the /90 opacity since the nav has backdrop-blur-md anyway. What is the correct explanation of why /90 and backdrop-blur-md work together?
options: backdrop-blur-md blurs what is behind the element. Without /90 opacity (or any transparency), there is nothing behind the element visible to blur — the effect requires partial transparency. The /90 makes the nav semi-transparent, and backdrop-blur-md blurs the page content showing through.
backdrop-blur-md does the same thing as /90 — they are redundant and one can be removed
The /90 is needed for dark mode only — in light mode, the browser handles transparency automatically
backdrop-blur-md requires the element to have exactly 90% opacity — other values cause the blur to not render
questions.answer: backdrop-blur-md blurs what is behind the element. Without /90 opacity (or any transparency), there is nothing behind the element visible to blur — the effect requires partial transparency. The /90 makes the nav semi-transparent, and backdrop-blur-md blurs the page content showing through.
questions.explanation: The frosted-glass effect is achieved by two cooperating properties: (1) partial opacity creates a window into the element's background — the page scrolling beneath the nav shows through; (2) backdrop-blur blurs specifically what is behind/beneath the element. A fully opaque element (bg-gray-900 without /90) would show no background at all — the backdrop-blur has nothing to blur because the solid background blocks all content behind it.

questions.prompt: The features grid uses grid-cols-[repeat(auto-fill,minmax(280px,1fr))]. A colleague suggests replacing it with grid-cols-1 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3. What is lost with the breakpoint-based approach?
options: The auto-fill approach adapts to any container width — at 600px it shows 2 columns, at 900px it shows 3, at 1200px it shows 4. Breakpoints create fixed jumps tied to viewport width, not the grid's available space.
The breakpoint approach generates more CSS classes and increases bundle size
auto-fill is required for dark mode to work correctly on grid items
The breakpoint approach prevents group-hover effects on grid items
questions.answer: The auto-fill approach adapts to any container width — at 600px it shows 2 columns, at 900px it shows 3, at 1200px it shows 4. Breakpoints create fixed jumps tied to viewport width, not the grid's available space.
questions.explanation: The repeat(auto-fill, minmax(280px, 1fr)) pattern is responsive to the grid's available space, not the viewport width. If this grid is ever placed in a narrower container (a sidebar, a modal, a two-column layout), it adapts automatically — the breakpoint approach would not, because md: and lg: are viewport breakpoints that don't know the grid's available width. auto-fill is the container-aware alternative to viewport breakpoints for intrinsically responsive grids.

questions.prompt: After shipping the enterprise page, a principal engineer reviews the code and notes: 'Every hardcoded indigo-600 in this file is a token violation.' You argue the Tailwind palette IS the token system. The principal disagrees. Who is correct and why?
options: The principal is correct — indigo-600 is a palette primitive. A semantic token like --color-primary: var(--color-indigo-600) separates intent from implementation, enabling rebrand by changing one value instead of find-and-replacing every indigo-600 occurrence.
You are correct — the Tailwind palette provides a token system out of the box and semantic tokens add unnecessary abstraction
Both are correct — it depends on whether the team needs rebranding, which is a business decision not a technical one
The principal is correct but only for colours that appear more than 5 times — one-off uses of palette primitives are acceptable
questions.answer: The principal is correct — indigo-600 is a palette primitive. A semantic token like --color-primary: var(--color-indigo-600) separates intent from implementation, enabling rebrand by changing one value instead of find-and-replacing every indigo-600 occurrence.
questions.explanation: The Tailwind palette provides primitives (named colour values), not semantic tokens. Semantic tokens encode intent: --color-primary means 'the primary action colour'. Palette primitives encode value: indigo-600 means 'indigo at shade 600'. When the brand changes from indigo to violet, every bg-indigo-600 in the codebase must be found and updated. With bg-primary backed by --color-primary: var(--color-indigo-600), you change one line. This is not over-engineering — it is the fundamental difference between a maintainable token system and a codebase that is expensive to rebrand.
